messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 50

He is a 67-year-old Latin American man who has spent most of his life presenting himself as composed, careful, and difficult to rattle. As a prosecutor, he has built a career around order, evidence, and controlled language. He is the kind of man who arrives early, dresses neatly, and speaks in measured sentences. People at work know him as steady. Few would guess how long he has been carrying the memory that now governs so much of his inner life.

The trauma occurs years ago, at a point in his life when he is already established in his profession and married. He does not speak about it easily, even now. What happened to him is sexual assault, and what stays with him is not only the violence of the act but the humiliation, the sudden loss of power, and the sense that the world became unsafe in a way he had never before imagined. In the immediate aftermath, he does what many men like him do: he says very little, pushes through, and tries to return to functioning as if nothing has happened. He tells himself that what matters is getting back to work, back to routine, back to being useful. For a while, he succeeds outwardly. Internally, he begins to live with a constant alertness that he cannot explain to others.

Over time, the memory refuses to stay in the past. He finds that certain sounds, smells, and situations bring it back with a force that surprises him. He becomes tense in crowded places and uneasy when he is unable to see who is behind him. He notices himself checking locks more than once, scanning exits, and sitting with his back to the wall when possible. At work, in courtrooms and conference rooms, he keeps careful control, but his concentration slips at unexpected moments. A phrase from a case, a smell in an elevator, the sound of a door closing too hard can pull him into a state of dread that is difficult to shake. He may look calm, but inside he is bracing.

His sleep is not restorative. He falls asleep tired and wakes early, often with his mind already racing. Nightmares leave him sweaty and disoriented, and on the worst mornings he lies still for a few minutes trying to reorient himself before he can face the day. He has learned to keep his reactions private. If he feels his chest tighten in court or his hands go cold while listening to testimony, he tightens his jaw and continues. At times he is startled by how quickly his mood changes; he becomes irritable with minor disruptions and later feels ashamed of his sharpness. He is aware of a growing distance between himself and other people, even those he loves. Since his wife’s death, that distance has become more pronounced. Her absence removes one of the few places where he used to relax, and now his evenings are often solitary and quiet in a way that feels heavy rather than restful.

He also carries a persistent sense of self-blame that he does not readily name. He questions what he could have done differently, whether he should have been stronger, whether his silence somehow allowed the experience to define him. As a prosecutor, he is practiced at believing facts and assembling narratives, but with this experience he has never been able to create a story that feels fair. Instead, he revisits it in fragments, each time feeling the same mixture of anger, shame, and helplessness. He remains functional in many areas, and colleagues continue to rely on him, but it costs him more than anyone sees.

He comes to therapy only after several months in which the burden becomes harder to contain. The tipping point is not a dramatic collapse but a gradual realization that he is spending too much energy avoiding reminders, losing sleep, and forcing himself through each day. What finally brings him in is the fear that he is no longer able to keep this hidden from himself, even if he has managed to hide it from everyone else.
